# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: Promise, Pitfalls, and a Changing Landscape

## Rationale and early enthusiasm

Permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES) transformed percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) but left a residual concern: a retained metallic frame that constrains the vessel, abolishes vasomotion and adaptive remodeling, and serves as a chronic nidus for inflammation, neoatherosclerosis, and late thrombosis. Despite improvements with the evolution from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents and then to DES, there remains a 2% to 3% per year incidence of stent-related events beyond 1 year regardless of stent type, and the pathogenesis may relate to the presence of a metallic frame, which distorts and constrains the vessel, limits vasomotion and adaptive vascular remodeling, and serves as a nidus for chronic inflammation, neoatherosclerosis, thrombosis, and strut fracture. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to provide transient mechanical support and drug delivery, then disappear, theoretically restoring vascular physiology and reducing very late adverse events [1].

The first-in-human ABSORB Cohort A study established proof of concept. A fully bioabsorbable drug-eluting coronary stent that scaffolds the vessel wall when needed and then disappears once acute recoil and constrictive remodeling have subsided has theoretical advantages; the bioabsorbable everolimus-eluting stent has a backbone of poly-L-lactic acid that provides support and a coating of poly-D,L-lactic acid that controls release of everolimus. [2] Thirty patients with a single de-novo lesion were followed for 2 years, and at 2 years the stent was bioabsorbed, had vasomotion restored and restenosis prevented, and was clinically safe. [3]

## Randomized evidence: the ABSORB program

A series of randomized trials compared the Absorb BVS with the cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting Xience stent (EES). The ABSORB II trial provided the first medium-term randomized data, but it did not meet its co-primary endpoints of superior vasomotor reactivity and non-inferior late luminal loss, and a higher rate of device-oriented composite endpoint due to target vessel myocardial infarction was observed in the Absorb group. [4] In ABSORB Japan, although BVS may theoretically provide superior long-term results compared with metallic DES, whether BVS are as safe and effective as metallic DES prior to complete bioresorption was unknown. [5] The pivotal ABSORB III trial then established 1-year non-inferiority for target lesion failure [6], but longer follow-up was sobering: 3-year adverse event rates were higher with BVS than EES, particularly target vessel myocardial infarction and device thrombosis. [7] Reassuringly, the 5-year analysis showed that cumulative adverse event rates were increased after BVS compared with EES, but the period of excess risk for BVS ended at 3 years, coincident with complete scaffold resorption. [8]

Patient-level pooled analyses corroborated these signals. A 1-year pooled meta-analysis of the ABSORB randomized trials examined early outcomes [9], a 2-year individual-patient-data meta-analysis of seven trials confirmed an excess of scaffold thrombosis [10], and the 3-year individual-patient-data analysis demonstrated that BVS compared with cobalt-chromium EES resulted in higher 3-year rates of target lesion failure (11.7% versus 8.1%), driven by greater target vessel myocardial infarction. [11] An early meta-analysis of randomized trials likewise found comparable efficacy but a higher thrombosis risk [12], as did mid-term [13] and seven-trial weighted analyses [14], and a more recent synthesis concluded that BVS were designed to replace conventional DES, but this meta-analysis of 17 randomized trials shows them to be inferior in safety and efficacy out to 5 years, driven by an elevated rate of stent thrombosis. [15].

## Real-world experience and the scaffold thrombosis problem

The all-comers AIDA trial tempered enthusiasm. There was no significant difference between groups in the primary outcome of target-vessel failure, but treatment with the bioresorbable scaffold was associated with a significantly higher incidence of overall and very late device thrombosis than the metallic stent through 2 years. [16], a finding sustained at 3 years [17] and through final 5-year follow-up [18]. Dedicated thrombosis meta-analyses confirmed that the excess risk of BVS relative to EES for stent thrombosis through 2 years was significant. [19], and a network meta-analysis of 91 trials found that patients treated with the Absorb BVS had a significantly higher risk of definite or probable scaffold thrombosis compared with metallic DES, and the risk of very late thrombosis was highest with the Absorb BVS among comparators. [20] Mechanistic and registry work attributed much of this risk to thick struts, malapposition, underexpansion, and suboptimal technique [21,22].

## Refining technique: ABSORB IV and COMPARE-ABSORB

Recognizing that technique mattered, ABSORB IV mandated optimized implantation. Polymeric BVS implanted with optimized technique in an expanded patient population resulted in non-inferior 30-day and 1-year rates of target lesion failure and angina compared with metallic DES. [23] At 5 years, the everolimus-eluting BVS was associated with slightly increased rates of target lesion failure and device thrombosis compared with metallic DES during the first 3 years prior to complete bioresorption. [24] In high-restenosis-risk patients, COMPARE-ABSORB met non-inferiority for TLF at one year, but BVS carried a higher risk of device thrombosis and target vessel myocardial infarction than EES. [25], and at 7 years BVS did not demonstrate superiority compared with DES. [26] The final ABSORB program report concluded that the period of excess risk for the first-generation Absorb BVS ended at 3 years when polymer resorption is complete, after which event rates were comparable or lower, and that further studies with improved scaffolds and techniques are required. [27]

## Newer-generation devices

Attention has shifted to thinner-strut and metallic-resorbable designs. The magnesium-based sirolimus-eluting Magmaris scaffold in BIOSOLVE-II achieved an in-segment late lumen loss of 0.27 ± 0.37 mm at 6 months. [28] Thinner-strut sirolimus-eluting polymeric scaffolds such as Firesorb in FUTURE-II were studied against EES [29], and the third-generation magnesium scaffold DREAMS 3G in BIOMAG-I showed a low target lesion failure rate of 2.6% at one year with no cardiac death, myocardial infarction, or scaffold thrombosis reported. [30]

## Conclusion

First-generation BVS did not fulfill their promise, with consistent early excess thrombosis and target-vessel infarction attributable to thick struts and implantation technique. Whether thinner-strut polymeric and resorbable-metal scaffolds, implanted with rigorous technique, can finally deliver the long-term benefit of a "leave-nothing-behind" strategy remains an open and actively investigated question.
